extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians and MathOverflow/math.stackexchange users (current or potential participants)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and normative remarks about how mathematicians should participate in MathOverflow (and similar Q&A): views on badges/reputation, anonymity, posting behaviour, and technical/UI preferences. The page is an opinion piece plus community comments addressing contributing, voting, and presentation norms on MO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gamification / remove 'silly' badges
rubrics_metrics.description: The very idea of badges is already hilarious; seeing lists of badges makes it hard for some to take the site seriously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design should avoid puerile or silly gamification elements (badge names like 'Necromancer'). Options: remove such badges, provide a user preference to hide them, or use adblock/CSS rules to hide badge UI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make reputation visibility optional
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no good reason that a user's reputation score should be publicly viewable at all; users should be able not to see others' reputations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add a user preference so reputations and badges are hidden from the viewer; full opt-out (so others can't see your rep) may be infeasible, but per-user hiding is feasible and was suggested on Meta.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain reputation as a mechanism for privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: Reputation has some sense: users who have contributed a lot earn the ability to do certain administrative tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reputation primarily as an access-control and moderation tool rather than a public status metric; make clear which privileges are tied to rep.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use community wiki to avoid gaining reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Making answers 'community wiki' means you will not accrue reputation from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you want to contribute without receiving points, post non-rep community-wiki answers where supported by the platform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participate pseudonymously or anonymously to focus readers on content
rubrics_metrics.description: Posting under random usernames or pseudonyms forces readers to attend to the mathematical content rather than the poster's identity or reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a pseudonym (distinct from true anonymity) if you want to avoid reputation-based judgments; note practical limits (e.g., unregistered users have voting restrictions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not game voting with multiple accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: The system detects suspicious voting patterns such as would be created by a person with multiple users voting for each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid creating or using multiple accounts to vote for yourself or coordinate votes; such patterns are monitored and can be penalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat votes as an imperfect proxy for mathematical value
rubrics_metrics.description: The correlation between interesting mathematics and votes is imperfect (some claim it is negative due to popularity effects); votes should be interpreted cautiously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't equate vote counts or reputation blindly with mathematical worth; consider other signals (clarity, novelty, depth) when judging content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write answers that teach and serve as public goods
rubrics_metrics.description: A good answer to a good question not only helps the questioner but teaches many future readers (the software gives MO questions high PageRank).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest a modest amount of expert time (possibly ~10 minutes) to craft clear, explanatory answers that will help future readers; aim for enduring pedagogical value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attempt to solve/think before asking
rubrics_metrics.description: Try not to ask every question that pops into your head; working out the answer yourself often yields substantial learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance the convenience of asking with the pedagogical value of struggling; refrain from posting trivial or impulsive questions to preserve the site's quality and your own learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lurking (observing) is a valuable contribution mode
rubrics_metrics.description: Lurking on MathOverflow is a precious experience: you can learn and witness interactions without actively posting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you prefer, learn by reading questions and answers rather than posting; lurking can be a legitimate, low-cost way to benefit and contribute indirectly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain at least one stable account for essential actions (comments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep one stable user with the minimum 50 points for commenting purposes (so you can leave comments if desired).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you plan to avoid accrual of rep by using throwaway accounts, retain a single stable account that has the threshold reputation required for commenting and other minimal interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer in comments to avoid accruing reputation (if desired)
rubrics_metrics.description: One strategy to avoid gaining points is to only answer in comment form, thereby avoiding receiving any points for answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comment-answers when you wish to help without accumulating reputation; be mindful of the platform's norms about using comments versus answers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use client-side UI fixes to elide unwanted elements
rubrics_metrics.description: If UI elements annoy you (badges, badgecounts), use adblock or custom CSS selectors to hide them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example Adblock/CSS rules were provided to hide badges on a user-page and in post signatures; this is a practical workaround if the platform doesn't provide preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize intrusive client-side scripts for simple interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive use of Javascript and AJAX for simple things (e.g., 'Show X more comments') is irritating and unnecessary to some users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer lightweight UI choices and allow users to opt out of running site scripts; reduce reliance on intrusive code for basic functionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand that reputation correlates more with participation than pure ability
rubrics_metrics.description: Reputation is generally more correlated with participation than mathematical prowess; it reflects activity as much as competence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating others, consider their participation level and activity patterns in addition to raw reputation; avoid overinterpreting rep as a measure of ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of trade-offs between openness and preserving the learning process
rubrics_metrics.description: Easy access to answers might reduce the incentive to struggle through problems, though opinions differ on whether this is harmful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider pedagogical trade-offs: encourage users (especially students) to attempt solutions themselves before asking, while recognizing that accessible answers also create large public benefits.
